newsitem.title: USA: Investigators wrap up King murder weapon probe.
newsitem.headline: Investigators wrap up King murder weapon probe.

text.p: A team of firearms investigators completed Thursday their analysis of bullet fragments taken from the body of slain civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr.

Investigators declined to comment on the results of their analysis. The team began its work Wednesday to determine whether the bullet taken from King's body was fired from the Remington rifle linked to his 1968 assasination at a Memphis, Tenn., hotel.

Robert Hathaway, the lead investigator and a University of Rhode Island criminalist, said the results would be sent to court officials in Tennessee within the next few weeks and be released publicly sometime later.
James Earl Ray, 69, confessed to killing King in 1969 but later recanted his story. His fingerprints were found on the rifle but it was never proven to be the murder weapon.

William Pepper, Ray's attorney, said if this week's tests show that the fatal bullet was not fired from the rifle, the court could set aside Ray's guilty plea and grant him a new trial. Ray is terminally ill with liver disease.
The bullet analysis was the second phase of a probe that began last week at a University of Rhode Island crime lab, where investigators test fired the rifle.
The analysis was done at CamScan USA in Cranberry Township, Pennsylvania, using a high-power microscope. The purpose of the probe was to either prove or exclude the rifle as the murder weapon.
Hathaway had said Wednesday at a news conference that the tests could come up inconclusive.
Ray's defence team contends that Ray was not the shooter, but that he gave the rifle to an unknown gun runner the night before the murder and never saw it again.
Under Tennesee law, a case can be re-opened if there is a reasonable possibility that technology that did not exist at the time of a crime may be able to prove a person's innocence.
